Paver Driveways · Lake Nona, FL

Paver Driveways in Lake Nona

A paver driveway in Lake Nona runs $10–$30 per sq ft installed as of October 2026. The city's engineering permit covers the material the same way it covers plain concrete, but in villages such as NorthLake Park, a color or paver change needs the neighborhood association's sign-off before the city application even goes in.

By the Opera Concrete & Pavers estimating team · Updated October 1, 2026

Replacing a paver driveway in an established Lake Nona village, worked out in square feet

Picture a home in one of Lake Nona's earlier-built sections relaying 480 square feet of driveway, a single-car-plus-guest-parking layout, in a different paver color than the original. Pricing that out at $10–$30 sq ft installed puts the job somewhere between $5,760 and $14,400, with the paver choice and base depth moving the number within that band, and the neighborhood's own architectural review typically scheduled before the crew's start date is confirmed.

NorthLake Park's rule: approval first, work second

In NorthLake Park, one of the community's first neighborhoods, homeowners “MUST obtain ARC approval prior to any work being started,” and skipping that step risks a modification violation that can cost more to fix after the fact than it would have to clear beforehand (NorthLake Park at Lake Nona, Community Portal). A paver driveway replacement, a color swap or widening an existing apron all count as the kind of exterior change that rule is written to catch, separate from whatever the city's own engineering permit requires.

An apron that meets the right-of-way has its own rules

The strip of driveway between the edge of a property and the street, often called the apron, usually sits inside a right-of-way the city or county controls rather than the homeowner. Florida law keeps a local government from requiring a license just to install a driveway, but that exemption covers the license, not the permit: a local government can still require a permit for work that touches its right-of-way. On a Lake Nona project where the apron crosses into that right-of-way, checking which department reviews that specific strip, separate from the rest of the driveway, is worth doing before the base crew ever shows up.

The city doesn't treat pavers more lightly than poured concrete

Orlando reviews a paver driveway under the identical engineering permit it uses for concrete, which is a heavier process than unincorporated Orange County applies to the same material (City of Orlando, Residential Permitting Requirements). On a Lake Nona lot, that city review runs alongside, not instead of, whichever village's architectural board also has to sign off, so a homeowner is generally clearing two separate approvals rather than one.

What a 98 percent Proctor reading actually means for a Lake Nona driveway

ICPI calls for the compacted subgrade and the aggregate base under a driveway to reach at least 98 percent of standard Proctor density, tested against ASTM D698, with vehicular areas held to the stricter modified Proctor instead. That number comes from a plate compactor working the base in lifts of 4 to 6 inches, not one pass over the whole excavation. Skipping a lift, or compacting a lift that's too thick, is how a base looks finished on the surface and still settles under Lake Nona traffic within a season. The spec also sets a surface tolerance of plus or minus three-eighths of an inch over 10 feet, tighter than it sounds once pavers sit on top of it.

What an HOA can and can't require before you start

An HOA's authority to approve a driveway's look exists only to the extent its declaration or published guidelines actually say so, and Florida law requires that authority to be used reasonably, with a written denial that cites the specific rule being enforced. As of the 2026 statutes, an HOA also can't require a government-issued building permit as a prerequisite just to review a project, which separates the association's own approval step from the city or county's separate permitting process. A Lake Nona homeowner inside an HOA is dealing with two different approvals that don't have to happen in a fixed order, and confusing the two is a common way a paver driveway project stalls before it starts.

What a crew checks before a single paver goes down

By the time the first paver is set, the base underneath has already been checked against two separate numbers: compaction density, tested to at least 98 percent of standard Proctor for a driveway, and surface tolerance, held to plus or minus three-eighths of an inch over a 10-foot span. Both checks happen before the bedding sand is even screeded, because fixing a low spot in the base is straightforward and fixing one after the pavers are set is not. On a Lake Nona job, that inspection step is the quiet middle of the process, sandwiched between the excavation everyone notices and the finished surface everyone sees, and it's the part that decides how the driveway looks in two years, not two days.

What efflorescence needs from you: nothing

The whitish bloom that can show up on new concrete pavers within the first couple of months doesn't call for a cleaner, a sealer, or a change in routine, because ICPI's spec is clear that it doesn't affect the structural performance of the pavers at all. It tends to fade on its own with normal weather and traffic, and scrubbing at it or sealing over it early can trap it rather than help it clear, so the honest advice for a Lake Nona driveway showing this in its first season is to keep up the normal sweeping and let it wear off. Treating it as a maintenance problem instead of a normal early-life process is the only real mistake available here.

Frequently asked questions

Does a paver driveway in Lake Nona need HOA approval even if the city already permits it?

In villages such as NorthLake Park, yes. The city's engineering permit and the neighborhood's own architectural review are two separate approvals, and starting work before the HOA signs off can mean a modification violation.

Does switching from concrete to pavers change the city permit process in Lake Nona?

No. Orlando reviews pavers under the same engineering permit category it uses for poured concrete, rather than a lighter process the way unincorporated Orange County does.

Do all Lake Nona neighborhoods run the same architectural review?

No. NorthLake Park, Laureate Park and other villages each run their own association, so the specific approval steps and timelines for a paver driveway can differ from one Lake Nona street to the next.
